Once upon a time, in a kingdom far beyond the mountains, there was a young cartographer named Elin who had spent her whole life drawing maps of places she had never seen. Her father had been a sailor, and every evening he would describe the coastlines, the harbors, the islands shaped like sleeping animals, and the currents that could carry a ship halfway around the world in a single season. Elin listened, and she drew. When she was seventeen, her father did not come back from his last voyage. The harbor master said the ship had been lost in a storm near the Glass Islands, a place that appeared on none of the official charts. But Elin had drawn the Glass Islands a hundred times, exactly as her father had described them, and she knew something the harbor master did not: the islands were real, and the storm that took her father's ship came every year in the same month, from the same direction. A transformer language model processes a sequence of tokens. Each token is mapped to a vector by an embedding table, and the vectors pass through a stack of layers. Each layer applies self-attention, in which every position computes a weighted average of the value vectors of earlier positions, followed by a feed-forward network applied to each position independently.
